column3: Employee-Handbook,"[115, 117, 116, 130, 249, 118, 138]","## Daily Task Management – How It Should Work for Different Age Groups & Classes

column1: Below is a **step‑by‑step description** of the daily‑task workflow that satisfies every rule mentioned in the project context. The flow is broken down by **class range** and **age**, and it also highlights the required **portal access**, **visibility restrictions**, and **privacy safeguards**.
### 1. Core Principles (Applicable to All Users)

column3: Detail
The system presents a separate portal view for each class/age group after login.
Only students **10 years old or older** may see the Daily Task section.

- **Teachers** create tasks for **Classes 1‑4**.
- **Students** (Class 5 + ) create their own tasks.

- **Classes 5‑7**: can **enter** tasks but **cannot view** any tasks (including their own).
- **Classes 8 +**: can **enter** *and* **view** their own tasks.
Personal information (e.g., name, age, gender, verification doc) is **not displayed** for any student **below 10th standard** (i.e., < Class 10).
Architecture must support **≈ 1 500 students** over the next 5 years, with the ability to extend server storage on approval.

column1: > **Note:** The “age ≥ 10” rule is the gating condition for *any* student to see the Daily Task module, regardless of class. If a student is younger than 10 y (even if in Class 5‑7), the module is hidden.
### 3. Detailed Interaction Flow
#### 3.1 Teacher Portal (Classes 1‑4)
1. **Login** → Teacher dashboard.
2. **Select Class** (1‑4) → “Daily Tasks” tab.
3. **Create / Edit Task**:
- Title, description, due date, optional attachment.
- Click **Save** → task stored in **Daily Data** table.
4. **No student visibility**: Since students in these classes cannot access the Daily Task module, the tasks remain teacher‑only.
#### 3.2 Student Portal – Classes 5‑7
1. **Login** → Student dashboard (age ≥ 10).
2. **Daily Tasks** button appears **only as “Enter Task”** (no “View” option).
3. **Enter Task** form → fill fields (title, description, optional self‑set deadline).
4. **Submit** → system stores the entry linked to the student’s ID.
5. **Confirmation** toast appears; the form resets.
6. **No task list** is shown; the student cannot view any tasks (including their own).
#### 3.3 Student Portal – Classes 8 +
1. **Login** → Student dashboard.
2. **Daily Tasks** tab shows two sub‑tabs:
- **Enter Task** (same as above).
- **My Tasks** – a read‑only list of the student’s own entries.
3. **Enter Task** → same flow as 5‑7.
4. **My Tasks** → displays:
- Task title, description, creation date, due date, status (Pending/Completed).
- Option to mark as **Completed** (optional reward system).
5. **Data isolation**: The list is filtered by the logged‑in student’s unique ID; no cross‑class data is exposed.
### 4. Privacy & Security Controls

column3: Implementation
At registration, capture **Date of Birth**; enforce the “≥ 10 y” rule before rendering the Daily Task UI.
Backend middleware checks **user.role** (teacher / student) and **user.class** to decide which API endpoints are reachable.
When generating any report or UI that could expose personal fields, hide **Name, Age, Gender, Verification Document** for students below Class 10.
Every task creation, edit, or view action is logged with timestamp, user ID, and IP for compliance.
Daily task entries are stored in a **partitioned table** keyed by class and year, allowing easy horizontal scaling to support 1 500+ students.

column2: Employee-Handbook,"[117, 118, 116, 115, 224, 222, 221]","## Complaint & SOS System – Student‑Facing Functionality

column1: Below is a concise, step‑by‑step description of how the **complaint** and **SOS** features are expected to work for students, based entirely on the meeting notes.
### 1. Entry Points on the Student Page

column3: Purpose
column4: Visibility

column3: Opens the **complaint / help** form where a student can raise an issue, give feedback, or send a compliment.
column4: Available to all logged‑in students.

column3: Triggers an emergency alert that is instantly sent to the designated coordinator.

column1: ### 2. Complaint Workflow
1. **Student submits a complaint** via the **Get Help** form.
2. **Routing of the complaint** (as defined by the requirements):
- **First level:** **Admin** receives the complaint.
- **Second level:** **Warden** receives a copy (after admin processing).
- **Third level:** **Secondary Admin** is also notified.
3. **Teacher approval (Partham side)**
- Before the complaint is forwarded to the **Warden**, a **teacher must approve** it.
- This step ensures that academic staff validates the relevance/validity of the issue.
4. **Escalation if unresolved**
- If the complaint remains **unresolved** after the initial handling, the system automatically **escalates** it to a **second‑level complaint** (e.g., higher‑level admin or senior warden).
5. **Outcome handling**
- Once resolved, the student receives a notification (via the system’s general notification module).
> **Key Points**
> - The flow guarantees **multiple oversight layers** (Admin → Teacher → Warden → Secondary Admin).
> - **Escalation** prevents complaints from being ignored.
### 3. Disciplinary Reporting (Teacher‑initiated)
- **Teachers** can directly **report misbehaving students** to the **Warden** through a dedicated “Disciplinary Reporting” option.
- This is separate from the student‑initiated complaint flow but uses the same backend routing to the Warden.
### 4. Compliment Feature
- Students may also send **positive feedback/compliments**.
- These are routed **only to the Admin** (no teacher approval or escalation needed).
### 5. SOS (Emergency) Feature

column4: Recipient
column5: Notification Method

column3: System generates an **alert** containing the student’s ID, location (if available), and timestamp.
column4: **Coordinator** (designated emergency contact)
column5: **Email** is sent automatically; the admin portal also shows the alert in the **SOS Monitoring** section.

column3: SOS alerts appear in real‑time on the **Admin SOS Monitoring** page for quick response.
column4: Admin staff can view and act on the alert.
column5: In‑app notification + email.

column1: - The SOS flow is **instantaneous** – no intermediate approvals are required, ensuring rapid response in emergencies.
### 6. Supporting Admin & Warden Tools
- **Warden Dashboard** (suggested by Adhik Sir) – displays incident reports, SOS alerts, and escalated complaints.
- **Role‑Based Access** – ensures only authorized personnel (Warden, Admin, Secondary Admin) can view or act on specific complaints/SOS alerts.
- **Complaint Escalation System** – built into the workflow to automatically promote unresolved issues.
### 7. End‑to‑End Example
1. **Student A** clicks **Get Help**, writes “Leaking faucet in bathroom”.
2. System logs the complaint and sends it to **Admin**.
3. **Teacher** reviews and **approves** the complaint.
4. Approved complaint is forwarded to the **Warden** and **Secondary Admin**.
5. Warden resolves the issue (maintenance fixed).
6. Student receives a **notification** confirming resolution.
If the warden does not close the ticket within the defined SLA, the system **escalates** the complaint to a higher authority automatically.
### 8. Summary
- **Get Help** → multi‑level routing with teacher approval → escalation if needed.
- **SOS** → immediate email alert to coordinator + real‑time admin monitoring.
- **Disciplinary reports** and **compliments** have dedicated, simpler paths.
- All actions are tracked and visible through role‑specific dashboards (Admin, Warden).
These mechanisms together provide a **transparent, accountable, and rapid response** system for student concerns and emergencies.",8,7,8,9.611,1,1.0,0.2857,1.0,1.0

column2: IT-Security-Policy,"[115, 117, 114, 116, 153, 168, 118]","## Design Principles for Younger Students (Classes 1‑7)

column3: What it means for the UI/UX
column4: Why it was chosen

column3: Layout, icons, and language are tailored to a 5th‑standard reading level (large buttons, minimal text, bright colours).
column4: Ensures younger learners can navigate without confusion.

column3: Clear, linear navigation paths; “Back” and “Home” icons are always visible; tasks are presented one‑step‑at‑a‑time.
column4: Reduces cognitive load and prevents getting lost in the portal.

column3: Tasks are short, gamified where possible, and use drag‑and‑drop or tap interactions rather than complex forms.
column4: Keeps younger students engaged and encourages regular use.

column3: Badges, points, or small virtual stickers are awarded for completing daily tasks or well‑being questionnaires.
column4: Provides positive reinforcement, especially important for early grades.

column3: Teachers are the sole data providers for classes 1‑4; students in these grades do not enter or edit their own daily‑task data.
column4: Guarantees data accuracy and protects younger children from accidental mistakes.

column3: Personal identifiers (full name, gender, verification documents) are hidden from any viewable pages for students below 10th standard.
column4: Aligns with the “Student Data Privacy” rule that personal info must not be visible to younger users.

column3: A new quote is automatically displayed each day on the home screen; no manual interaction required.
column4: Adds a positive, predictable element that younger students can look forward to.

column3: 20‑25 pre‑written questions (provided by the curriculum lead) are presented in a child‑friendly format (e.g., smiley‑face rating).
column4: Encourages self‑reflection without overwhelming the child.

column3: A gentle, periodic pop‑up or icon nudges the student to drink water.
column4: Supports health habits in an unobtrusive way.

column1: ## Restrictions When Availing Earned / Privilege Leave
- **Advance notice**: Must be given **≥ 7 full working days** before the leave start date.

- **Accrual limit**: 1 EL/PL day is credited for every **20 working days** completed.

- **Pro‑ration**:
• **Mid‑year joiners** receive a **pro‑rated** entitlement from the date of joining to 31 Dec.
• **Resigning employees** have their balance calculated up to the last working day; any excess taken is adjusted in the final settlement.

- **Combination with other leaves**:

• **EL/PL cannot be combined with Casual Leave**.
- **Carry‑forward**: Unused Earned Leave may be **carried forward** to the next calendar year **subject to a maximum of 45 days**. (Privilege Leave follows the same rule unless otherwise specified.)
- **Encashment**: Encashable leave (if any) is calculated as **Monthly Gross ÷ 26 × Encashable Leave days** and is fully taxable.

column2: Employee-Handbook,"[122, 125, 124, 126, 256, 211, 128]","## Leave Entitlement for Mid‑Year Joinees & Resigning Employees

column1: The policy treats **new hires** and **employees who leave** on a **pro‑rata** basis – i.e., they receive a proportion of the annual leave that corresponds to the part of the calendar year they actually work.
Below is a breakdown of how each leave category is calculated.
### 1. Casual Leave (CL) – 7 days per year

column3: How the entitlement is calculated

Entitlement = 7 days × (Number of days worked in the calendar year ÷ 365).
For a July‑1 start, roughly **½ × 7 ≈ 3.5 days** (rounded according to company rounding rules).

Entitlement = 7 days × (Days worked in the year up to the last working day ÷ 365).
Any unused CL is **not carried forward** and is **not encashable**.

• Maximum 3 CL can be taken in a month.

• No carry‑forward or encashment.

column1: ### 2. Sick Leave (SL) – 7 days per year

column3: How the entitlement is calculated

Entitlement = 7 days × (Days worked ÷ 365).
Example: joining 1 July → **≈ 3.5 days** of SL.

Entitlement = 7 days × (Days worked ÷ 365).
Unused SL lapses at year‑end; it is **not encashable**.

• Minimum 0.5 day, maximum 7 days per occurrence (paid).
• For absences > 2‑3 days a medical certificate is normally required.
• SL **can be appended** to Earned/Privilege Leave.

column1: ### 3. Earned / Privilege Leave (EL/PL)

column3: How the entitlement is calculated

Example: joining 1 July → ~ 92 working days → **≈ 4.6 EL days** (rounded per policy).

Any **excess** EL taken beyond the pro‑rated amount is **deducted** from the final settlement.

• EL can be **combined** with Sick Leave.
• Unused EL may be **carried forward** (max 45 days).
• Encashment formula (if applicable): `Encashable Amount = (Monthly Gross / 26) × Number of Encashable Leave`.
• Encashment is fully taxable.

column2: IT-Security-Policy,"[111, 112, 113, 109, 110, 150, 153]","## Technical Factors that Exacerbated the Incident

column1: *(Beyond the primary firmware‑level timing calibration bug)*

column3: Specific Factor
column4: How It Contributed

column3: • Missing distributed drift anomaly alerts
column4: The clock‑drift was not detected early, allowing nanosecond‑scale drift to accumulate unchecked.

column3: • Lack of chaos testing for multi‑region clock desynchronization
column4: No simulated timing failures were exercised, so the system had no proven resilience to drift across regions.

column3: • Telemetry replay buffers configured below recommended capacity
column4: Limited buffer space caused loss of ordering information and increased latency when the backlog grew.

column3: • GPU inference autoscaling thresholds were too conservative
column4: Inference queues saturated (93 % utilization) and throttled AI models, reducing prediction confidence from 98.4 % to 71.2 %.

column3: • Apache Pulsar backlog peaked at 5.2 M events
column4: Backlog delayed telemetry propagation, worsening the timing mismatch and consensus errors.

column3: • CockroachDB consensus delay of 11.4 s
column4: Drift‑induced ordering inconsistencies slowed replication, further desynchronizing state across regions.

column3: • Redis cache invalidation spike (73 %)
column4: Frequent invalidations increased read latency and contributed to stale timing data being used by downstream services.

column3: • 18,204 failed synchronization checks
column4: High failure count indicated systemic timing verification breakdown, propagating errors to navigation calculations.

column3: • Under‑estimated distributed timing dependencies
column4: Architecture relied on tight clock alignment; the bug exposed this hidden coupling, amplifying downstream effects.

column3: • Existing monitoring emphasized service uptime rather than synchronization integrity
column4: Lack of metrics on clock health meant the drift went unnoticed until it manifested as large‑scale failures.

column3: • Insufficient multi‑region event ordering validation
column4: Pulsar streams and CockroachDB could not detect out‑of‑order events caused by drift, leading to inconsistent telemetry.

column1: ### Additional Observations from the Incident Report
- **Telemetry latency** rose to **18.6 seconds**, far beyond acceptable limits, directly impacting maneuver calculations.
- **GPU utilization** peaked at **97 %**, indicating that inference resources were a bottleneck.
- **Manual overrides** (6) and **near‑threshold collision alerts** (2) were triggered because the timing error corrupted collision‑prediction data.
### Summary

While the firmware bug was the root cause, a combination of **insufficient monitoring/alerting**, **inadequate testing**, **resource constraints** (replay buffers, GPU autoscaling), **messaging backlog**, **database consensus delays**, and **over‑reliance on uptime metrics** all compounded the problem, turning a timing drift into a full‑scale incident affecting 43 satellites.",5,4,5,7.277,1,1.0,0.2857,1.0,1.0

column1: - **What this means:**

- **Re‑insertion** → Sensor signals “worn” → System issues a play/resume command, picking up exactly where it left off.
3. **User Experience:** No extra taps or voice commands are required; the transition is automatic.

50,"If I'm creating a password for an iCIMS system, what minimum requirements do I need to meet?",medium,procedure,IT Security Policy,[161],IT-Security-Policy,"[206, 161, 156, 162, 163, 157, 149]","## Minimum Password Requirements for iCIMS Systems

57,"If my computer is suspected to have a virus, what actions does the IT Security Policy require?",hard,multi_section,IT Security Policy,"[173, 174]",IT-Security-Policy,"[173, 174, 204, 189, 156, 203, 147]","## Actions Required When a Computer Is Suspected of Having a Virus

column3: What You Must Do
column4: Policy Reference

column3:
• Inform the **IT Department** right away that you suspect a virus infection.
• Also report the incident to **Information Security** so it can be escalated to the **Security Incident Response Team (SIRT)**.
• Disconnect the computer from all network connections (wired, Wi‑Fi, VPN, etc.) to prevent spread.

• Allow the IT/InfoSec team to run an **up‑to‑date anti‑virus/anti‑malware scan** on the isolated system.
• Remove any detected malicious files and remediate the infection.
• Any USB drives, external disks, or other media that were attached to the infected computer must also be scanned and cleaned (or quarantined) before reuse.
• If the cleaning process cannot **definitively prove** that the virus has been removed, the system must be **completely wiped and re‑imaged** to a known clean master image.
• Users or subscribers whose data may have been exposed must be notified **as soon as reasonably possible**, following the organization’s Incident Response Procedures.
• The incident, actions taken, and any lessons learned should be recorded in the incident log (SIEM, Rapid7 IDR, etc.) for future audit and improvement.
column4: Implied by overall incident‑response framework (see 15.4.5).

column1: ### Summary Flow
1. **Detect suspicion** →
2. **Report immediately** (IT Dept & InfoSec → SIRT) →
3. **Isolate** the device from all networks →
4. **Run anti‑virus scan** and **clean** →
5. **If cleaning uncertain** → **Wipe & re‑image** →
6. **Notify impacted users** →
7. **Document** the incident.
### Key Points to Remember
- **Speed matters** – the faster you report, the quicker the isolation and containment can occur.
- **Do not attempt self‑remediation** (e.g., uninstalling software, deleting files) before the IT team takes control; this could destroy evidence needed for proper analysis.
- **All removable media** that touched the suspected system must be treated as potentially infected.
- **Full wipe/re‑image** is the fallback when the infection cannot be proven cleared.
> **If any of the above steps are unclear or you lack the means to perform them, contact the IT Help Desk or Information Security immediately for guidance.**",9,8,9,11.057,1,1.0,0.2857,1.0,1.0

58,What access control principle does the policy require users and administrators to follow when granting permissions?,medium,paraphrase,IT Security Policy,[176],IT-Security-Policy,"[176, 175, 177, 191, 164, 178, 166]","## Access‑Control Principle Required by the Policy

- **Least Privilege** – Users and administrators must be granted **only the permissions necessary to perform their job functions** and no more.

- **User Access Requests** (8.9.2.1) – Must request only the rights needed for the job.

- **Ongoing Management** (8.9.8, 8.9.9) – Periodic reviews and removal of unnecessary privileges ensure the principle remains in effect over time.

69,How do the Backup Policy and Disaster Recovery Policy work together to protect company data?,hard,comparison,IT Security Policy,"[172, 175]",IT-Security-Policy,"[172, 147, 171, 151, 149, 158, 202]","## How the **Backup Policy** and **Disaster Recovery (DR) Policy** Work Together to Protect Company Data

column3: Backup Policy (Section 6)
column4: Disaster Recovery Policy (Section 5)
column5: How They Complement Each Other

column3: Create and retain encrypted copies of data, applications, and server configurations so they can be recovered after a loss event.
column4: Define the processes, responsibilities, and testing cadence for restoring IT services and data after a disaster, aligning with business‑continuity goals.

column3:
• Daily backups for critical systems and any system that holds production Subscriber Data, Personal Data, or PII.
• Regular (unspecified) backups for all other data/applications.
column4:
• DR plans are **tested on a regular basis** as required by the Support & Maintenance Policy (SMP).
• Business‑continuity plan (which includes DR) is **tested at least once per calendar year**.

column3:
• All backups encrypted **at rest and in transit** per the Data Protection & Encryption Policy (AES‑256, TLS 1.2, etc.).
• Stored in a **physically and logically secure, geographically separate** location.
column4: • DR plans must consider **information‑security requirements**, ensuring that restored data remains protected (e.g., re‑applying encryption, access controls).

column3: Backups retained according to the Support and Maintenance Policy (SMP) and the iCIMS Data Retention Policy.
column4: Retention of DR documentation and test results is implied by the SMP; the policy does not specify separate retention rules.

column3: Implicitly validated by the requirement that backups be **encrypted** and stored securely; however, the policy does not mandate separate test cycles.
column4: **Explicit testing** of DR plans (including restoration from backups) is required regularly and at least annually, ensuring that backup data can actually be recovered.

column3: Guarantees that a recent, secure copy of critical data exists and can be accessed when needed.
column4: Guarantees that the organization knows **how** to retrieve and restore those copies quickly, minimizing downtime and data loss.

column1: ### Integrated Protection Flow
1. **Backup Creation**
- Automated, encrypted backups are taken daily for critical systems (Subscriber Data, PII, etc.).
- Backups are stored off‑site in a secure, separate location, meeting the encryption standards of the Data Protection & Encryption Policy.
2. **Backup Retention & Management**
- Retention schedules follow SMP and iCIMS Data Retention Policy, ensuring copies are kept for the required period.
3. **Disaster Occurs** (e.g., hardware failure, ransomware, natural disaster).
4. **Activation of DR Plan**
- The DR plan, aligned with the Business Continuity Plan, is triggered.
- It outlines **who** initiates recovery, **what** systems are prioritized, and **how** to retrieve the appropriate backup sets.
5. **Data Restoration**
- Using the encrypted backups, the DR team restores applications, data, and server configurations.
- Because backups are stored in a separate geographic location, the DR process can proceed even if the primary site is compromised.
6. **Verification & Testing**
- After restoration, the DR plan includes validation steps (e.g., integrity checks, functional testing).
- Regular testing (as required by the DR policy) confirms that backups are usable and that the restoration process meets recovery‑time objectives.
7. **Continuous Improvement**
- Test results feed back into both policies:
- **Backup Policy** may be refined (e.g., adjusting frequency or encryption methods).
- **DR Policy** may be updated to reflect lessons learned, ensuring future recoveries are faster and more reliable.
### Key Takeaways
- **Backup Policy** provides the *raw material* (secure, up‑to‑date copies of data) needed for recovery.
- **Disaster Recovery Policy** provides the *process* (plans, responsibilities, testing) to *use* those backups effectively when a disruption occurs.

- Together, they create a **defense‑in‑depth** strategy: data is protected both at rest (through encryption and secure storage) and in motion (through secure transmission), and the organization is prepared to **restore** that data quickly and securely, thereby maintaining business continuity.

> **Bottom line:** Without regular, encrypted backups, a DR plan would have nothing to restore; without a tested DR plan, backups might never be recovered in time. The two policies are interdependent and together ensure that company data remains confidential, available, and resilient against disasters.",5,3,6,12.153,1,0.5,0.1429,1.0,0.6131

column3: **Authorized software review & approval**

column5: Conduct a security review based on system criticality and data type; include free, shareware, open‑source, and SaaS products.

column3: **Prohibition of unauthorized/end‑of‑life software**
column4: 3.1‑3.6 – *Only authorized, supported, properly licensed software may be installed; end‑of‑life software is considered unauthorized*
column5: Verify that the software version is **supported** and **licensed**; remove any EOL components before release.

column3: **Timely remediation of high‑risk/zero‑day findings**
column4: 10.4.5 – *30 days for high‑risk critical and/or security vulnerabilities; 14 days for zero‑day vulnerabilities*
column5: Ensure any discovered high‑risk or zero‑day issues are **remediated within the stipulated timeframes** before the change proceeds to production.

column3: **Secure data‑in‑transit controls (if applicable)**
column4: 22.1 – *All data in transit must be encrypted or use an encrypted channel*
column5: Verify that any data moved as part of the change (e.g., configuration files, database migrations) uses approved encryption mechanisms.

column3: **Security awareness & training**
column4:
21.7 – *Awareness training regarding secure coding shall be conducted at least once per calendar year*
11.1 – *Security awareness training shall be conducted at least once per calendar year*
column5: Personnel involved in the change must have completed the required secure‑coding and security‑awareness training.

column1: ### Summary Flow (High‑Level Checklist)
1. **Code Management** – Store in version control.
2. **Secure Coding** – Follow OWASP Top 10 guidelines.
3. **QA & Security Testing** – Multi‑phase QA, vulnerability scans, fix severity 2+ findings.
4. **Data Handling** – Use synthetic/de‑identified data; encrypt any data in transit.
5. **Environment Controls** – Keep dev/test/prod segregated; enforce separation of duties.
6. **Change Control** – Submit change request, obtain security review/approval, document configuration changes.
7. **Authorization** – Verify software is licensed, supported, and not end‑of‑life.
8. **Remediation Timing** – Address high‑risk/zero‑day issues within 30/14 days respectively.
9. **Production Release** – Only production‑authorized personnel execute the change; developers/testers have no production access.
10. **Post‑Deployment Clean‑up** – Remove test data/accounts; confirm no residual test artefacts remain.

**If any of the above controls are missing from your current process, they must be added to satisfy the IT Security Policy before a software change can be deployed to production.**",4,2,5,15.973,1,1.0,0.1429,1.0,1.0

74,How does the IT Security Policy protect sensitive information both while it is stored and while it is transmitted?,medium,comparison,IT Security Policy,[158],IT-Security-Policy,"[158, 203, 156, 201, 167, 152, 202]","## How the IT Security Policy Protects Sensitive Information

The policy defines a set of technical and procedural controls that cover **both storage (data‑at‑rest)** and **movement (data‑in‑transit)** of sensitive information such as Personal Data, PII, SCI, and Subscriber Data.

column3: **Controls Specified in the Policy**
column4: **Purpose / Benefit**

column3:
• **AES‑256 encryption** for all sensitive data (1.1.1)
• **Bcrypt hashing** for stored passwords or other hashed values, with adaptive work factor (1.5)
• **Media sanitization** (NIST 800‑88) for disposed media, including shredding, burning, pulverizing, or overwriting (23.4)
• **Inventory & disposal logs** – audit trail for media handling, retained ≥ 90 days (23.4.2) and certificates of destruction kept ≥ 1 year (23.4.3)
• **Wireless‑network encryption** (e.g., WPA3) with separate SSIDs for corporate‑owned devices (1.6)
column4:
• Guarantees confidentiality even if storage media are stolen or lost.
• Protects against offline cracking (bcrypt) and rainbow‑table attacks.
• Ensures that retired media cannot be recovered, meeting regulatory “right to be forgotten” requirements.
• Provides traceability for media handling and disposal.
• Extends encryption to the wireless layer, preventing eavesdropping on Wi‑Fi traffic.

column3:
• **TLS 1.2** or **IPsec** for all network communications (1.2)
• **RSA/DSA key exchange** with ≥ 2048‑bit keys and ≥ 256‑bit digests (1.3)
• **Digital signatures** using RSA/DSS with ≥ 2048‑bit keys and ≥ 256‑bit digests (1.4)
• **VPN** usage (definition provided) to extend private networks over public links
• **Transfer of Information Policy** – mandates encryption of every data‑in‑transit flow and continuous monitoring of exchange channels (22.1)
• **Messaging Security Policy** – DLP monitoring on outbound email, virus/phishing scanning on inbound email, and requirement that approved messaging services provide encryption at rest *and* in transit plus audit trails (24.1‑24.3)
column4:
• TLS/IPsec provide confidentiality and integrity for web, API, and site‑to‑site traffic.
• Strong key‑exchange and signature algorithms protect against man‑in‑the‑middle and forgery attacks.
• VPNs create a protected tunnel when employees connect from untrusted networks.
• Continuous monitoring detects unauthorized releases and enforces DLP rules.
• Email and messaging controls prevent leakage of sensitive data and ensure that any communication channel used is cryptographically protected.

column1: ### Key Take‑aways
1. **Encryption is mandatory** for all sensitive data both at rest (AES‑256) and in transit (TLS 1.2 / IPsec).
2. **Strong cryptographic primitives** (RSA/DSA ≥ 2048 bits, SHA‑256‑like digests) are required for key exchange and digital signatures, ensuring authenticity and integrity.
3. **Password/secret storage** uses bcrypt, an adaptive hash with built‑in salting, to resist brute‑force and rainbow‑table attacks.
4. **Wireless environments** are not an exception; corporate Wi‑Fi must be encrypted and segmented by device type.
5. **Data disposal** follows NIST 800‑88 media‑sanitization guidelines, with documented audit trails to prove compliance.
6. **Transmission monitoring** (DLP, email scanning, approved messaging services) adds a layer of detection and policy enforcement beyond pure cryptography.

Together, these controls create a defense‑in‑depth posture that protects sensitive information whether it resides on disks, tapes, or other media, or travels across internal networks, the Internet, or wireless links.",4.5,2.5,5.5,11.98,1,1.0,0.1429,1.0,1.0

80,"Before sharing confidential company information with another employee, what responsibilities do I have?",medium,procedure,Employee-Handbook.pdf,[219],Employee-Handbook,"[219, 234, 235, 232, 218, 230, 236]","### Responsibilities Before Sharing Confidential Company Information with Another Employee

column3: **What You Must Do**
column4: **Why It Matters**

column3:
• Confirm that the other employee is **authorized** to receive the specific confidential data.
• Ensure the disclosure is **necessary for their job duties** (need‑to‑know basis).
column4: Prevents unauthorized access and limits exposure of sensitive information.

column3:
• Keep the confidential material **locked or otherwise protected** until it is handed over.
• Use **secure devices** (company‑approved, encrypted) to view or transmit the data.
• If the information is in paper form, **shred** any unnecessary copies after the transfer.
column4: Maintains the integrity and confidentiality of the data during handling.

column3: • Record **who** is receiving the information, **what** is being shared, **when**, and **for what purpose** (e.g., via a brief email or log entry).
column4: Provides an audit trail and demonstrates compliance with the policy.

column3:
• Share **only the portion** of the information that is required for the employee’s task.
• Avoid sending entire files or databases when a smaller excerpt will suffice.
column4: Reduces the risk of accidental over‑exposure.

column3: • Keep any physical documents **inside company premises** unless it is absolutely necessary to move them, and then ensure they are **securely transported** (e.g., sealed envelope, locked bag).
column4: Prevents loss or theft of confidential documents.

column3:
• Do **not** use the confidential information for personal benefit or profit.
• Do **not** replicate the data on insecure personal devices or cloud services.
column4: Aligns with the company’s prohibition on personal exploitation of confidential data.

column3:
• Use **company‑approved, encrypted channels** (e.g., secure email, internal file‑sharing system) for electronic transmission.
• Do **not** discuss confidential details in public areas, over unsecured networks, or via personal messaging apps.
column4: Ensures that the data remains protected during transmission.

column3: • If you are uncertain about the employee’s authorization or the appropriateness of the disclosure, **consult your manager, HR, or the PR/Legal department** before proceeding.
column4: Helps avoid accidental policy violations.

column1: #### Quick Checklist Before You Share
- [ ] Is the recipient **authorized** and does the request meet a **business need**?
- [ ] Is the information being shared **securely** (locked, encrypted, on a secure device)?
- [ ] Have you **limited** the data to only what is required?
- [ ] Have you **recorded** the transfer details for audit purposes?
- [ ] Are you using **company‑approved communication channels**?
- [ ] Have you **avoided** any personal use or storage on insecure devices?
- [ ] If any doubt remains, have you **asked for clarification** from a manager or HR?

Following these responsibilities ensures compliance with the company’s confidentiality and data‑protection policies and protects both the organization and you from potential breaches.",7,6,8,10.344,1,1.0,0.1429,1.0,1.0

82,"As someone representing the company on social media, what responsibilities do I have before posting important announcements?",hard,multi_section,Employee-Handbook.pdf,"[234, 235]",Employee-Handbook,"[234, 235, 210, 219, 239, 230, 229]","## Responsibilities Before Posting Important Announcements

83,"I'm dating someone who reports directly to me. According to the employee handbook, is this allowed?",easy,direct_lookup,Employee-Handbook.pdf,[237],Employee-Handbook,"[237, 238, 236, 210, 239, 212, 270]","## Short Answer
**No – the handbook does not allow you to date an employee who reports directly to you.**
## Relevant Policy Excerpts

column3: Quote from Handbook
column4: Interpretation

column3: “To avoid accusations of favoritism, abuse of authority and sexual harassment, **supervisors must not date their direct reports**. This restriction extends to every manager above an employee.”
column4: Direct‑report relationships are expressly prohibited for anyone in a supervisory role.

column3: “Fraternization refers to dating or being friends with your colleagues. In this policy, *dating* equals consensual romantic relationships and sexual relations. **Non‑consensual relationships constitute sexual violence and we prohibit them explicitly.**”
column4: While consensual dating among peers is allowed, the “Dating managers” rule overrides it when a supervisory line exists.

column3: “If you witness this kind of behavior, please report it to HR.”
column4: Violations should be reported and may trigger HR action.

column1: ## Why It’s Not Allowed
1. **Conflict of Interest** – A supervisor dating a direct report creates a real or perceived conflict of interest (favoritism, bias in performance reviews, promotions, etc.).
2. **Power Imbalance** – The supervisory role gives the manager authority over the employee’s job duties, compensation, and career progression, which can be seen as coercive or abusive.
3. **Company Policy** – The handbook explicitly bans such relationships to protect both parties and the organization from legal and ethical risks.
## What You Should Do
1. **Notify HR Immediately** – Even if the relationship is consensual, the policy requires disclosure so that appropriate steps (e.g., re‑assignment, transfer) can be taken.
2. **Avoid Workplace Interaction on Personal Matters** – Keep any personal discussions out of the work environment.
3. **Cooperate with Any Required Re‑assignment** – The handbook notes that if a manager and direct report become related, the company may need to transfer one of them to eliminate the reporting line.
## Bottom Line
- **Dating a direct report is prohibited** under the “Dating managers” policy.
- Failure to comply can lead to HR investigation, possible reassignment, and disciplinary action.
If you need guidance on how to proceed with disclosure or possible re‑assignment, contact your HR representative promptly.",6,4,8,9.014,1,1.0,0.1429,1.0,1.0

92,"As a manager starting disciplinary action against an employee, what process am I expected to follow?",hard,multi_section,Employee-Handbook.pdf,"[264, 265, 266]",Employee-Handbook,"[264, 265, 211, 268, 245, 214, 220]","## Disciplinary Action – Manager’s Expected Process
Below is the step‑by‑step procedure you should follow when you need to start a disciplinary action against an employee, based on the company policy you provided.

column3: **What to Do**
column4: **Key Points / Tips**

column3:
• Review the employee’s behavior or performance problem.
• Match the offense to the appropriate step in the progressive‑discipline ladder (e.g., minor dress‑code breach → Step 1; serious misconduct such as sexual harassment → Step 5).
column4:
• Use the “different offenses correspond to different steps” guidance.
• Consult HR or your manager if you are unsure about the severity.

column2: **2. Notify the Employee that Discipline is Starting**
column3:
• Tell the employee that a progressive‑discipline process is being launched.
• Explain that you will follow the company’s procedure and that HR will help clarify the steps.
column4:
• This communication is required before any formal step begins.
• It is **not** the same as routine performance feedback.

column3:
• Request HR’s assistance to:
    - Explain the full disciplinary procedure to the employee.
    - Provide any required documentation templates.
    - Ensure the process complies with legal and policy requirements.
column4: • HR involvement helps protect the company and the employee’s rights.

column3:
Follow the six‑step progressive‑discipline sequence, moving forward as needed:
1. **Verbal warning** – informal, documented conversation.
2. **Informal meeting with supervisor** – more detailed discussion, still informal.
3. **Formal reprimand** – written warning, signed by employee and manager.
4. **Formal disciplinary meeting** – formal sit‑down, may involve HR, employee can present their side.
5. **Penalties** – e.g., suspension, demotion, loss of privileges.
6. **Termination** – final step for cause or after repeated failures.
column4:
• **Managers may skip or repeat steps** at their discretion, but must still act **fairly, lawfully, and document every stage**.
• For serious offenses (e.g., sexual harassment) you may jump directly to Step 5 or Step 6.

column3:
• Write a brief summary of each conversation/meeting (date, participants, issues discussed, agreed actions).
• Have the employee sign the written documents where required.
• Store the records in the employee’s HR file.
column4: • Documentation is essential for defending the decision if a wrongful‑dismissal claim arises.

column3:
• After each step, give the employee a reasonable period to correct the behavior.
• Track progress and provide feedback.
• If improvement occurs, you may return to normal performance management.
column4: • Continuous monitoring shows good‑faith effort to help the employee succeed.

column3:
• If the employee corrects the issue, close the disciplinary file.
• If the problem persists, move to the next step (or, for severe cases, proceed directly to termination).
column4: • For **termination for cause**, ensure you have solid performance/disciplinary records to support the decision.

column3:
• Provide any required severance, accrued PTO, or other payouts per local law and company policy.
• Offer references only for employees who left in good standing.
column4: • Follow the “Leaving our company” section for details on payouts and references.

column1: ### Additional Considerations
- **At‑Will Employment (U.S.)** – While the company *may* terminate at any time without following every step, you are still required to act **fairly, lawfully, and document** the process.
- **Manager Discretion** – You can **skip** steps for very serious misconduct or **repeat** steps if the employee needs more time to improve.
- **HR Support** – Always involve HR early; they can help ensure compliance with local laws, union agreements, and internal policies.
- **Wrongful Dismissal Prevention** – Keep accurate, contemporaneous records of performance issues and disciplinary actions; this protects both the employee and the company.
### Quick Reference Checklist for Managers
1. **Assess the issue** → determine severity.
2. **Inform employee** that discipline is being initiated.
3. **Engage HR** for guidance and documentation.
4. **Execute the appropriate step** (verbal warning → termination).
5. **Document** every conversation/meeting.
6. **Monitor** improvement and provide feedback.
7. **Escalate** to the next step if needed.
8. **Complete termination** (if reached) with proper payouts and references.
Following this structured process will help you manage disciplinary actions consistently, fairly, and in line with company policy.",8,5,7,14.876,1,0.6667,0.2857,1.0,0.7654

1. **Report the incident** – Contact the designated internal point of contact (usually IT/Security) as soon as possible, but no later than 24 hours after the theft or damage occurs.
2. **Provide documentation** – Obtain a police affidavit (theft statement) and forward a copy to the company along with your incident report.
3. **Follow any additional instructions** – The company may request further details or steps (e.g., remote wipe, device tracking) after you report the event.
**Summary:**

The only policy in the provided material that explicitly mentions a **24‑hour** deadline is the **“Theft and damage of company equipment”** policy. It requires you to **inform the company within 24 hours** whenever a company‑issued device is stolen or damaged, and to submit a police affidavit as part of that reporting.",9,9,9,7.37,1,1.0,0.1429,1.0,1.0
98,"Which employee policy refers to '1.7 days per month', and what does that number represent?",easy,direct_lookup,Employee-Handbook.pdf,[256],Employee-Handbook
column2: Leave-Policy,"[256, 122, 125, 212, 211, 258, 210]","## Policy that mentions **“1.7 days per month”**

column2: IT-Security-Policy,"[250, 189, 212, 211, 210, 262, 269]","## “Two consecutive weeks” – What It Refers To

column1: The phrase **“two consecutive weeks”** appears in the **Remote Working** section of the employee handbook. It defines the **maximum amount of time an office‑based employee may work remotely in a single stretch**.
### Key Points of the Policy

column3: Details

Employees who are **new parents** or who have a **short‑term disability**.

Not covered by this two‑week rule; permanent remote workers must follow the standard security, confidentiality, and equal‑opportunity policies.

column1: ### How It Works in Practice
1. **Identify eligibility** – Confirm you are an office‑based employee and fall under one of the eligible categories (new parent or short‑term disability).
2. **Plan the dates** – Choose a continuous period that does not exceed 14 days.
3. **Submit the request** – Use the HRIS portal to file the request **≥ 7 days** before the start date.
4. **Manager approval** – Your manager will review and approve (or discuss alternatives) the request.

If you need remote work beyond the two‑week limit or for a different reason, you must **talk to your manager** to explore other arrangements, but the handbook’s explicit “two consecutive weeks” rule applies only to the scenario described above.",9,10,9,7.391,1,1.0,0.1429,1.0,1.0

101,I'm working remotely using a company laptop. What security and confidentiality responsibilities apply to me?,hard,multi_section,Employee-Handbook.pdf,"[219, 249, 255]",Employee-Handbook
column2: IT-Security-Policy,"[219, 250, 255, 232, 190, 254, 153]","## Security & Confidentiality Responsibilities for Remote Workers

column1: *Using a company‑issued laptop while working off‑site*

column3: What you must do
column4: Why it matters

column3:
• Keep all confidential information **locked or secured** at all times.
• View confidential data **only on the company laptop** (or other authorized secure devices).
• **Shred** paper documents that are no longer needed.
• Disclose information **only to authorized employees** and only when necessary.
• Do **not** take confidential documents off the company premises unless absolutely required and approved.
column4: Prevents accidental leaks and protects employee, customer, and business data.

column3:
• Do **not** use confidential information for personal benefit or profit.
• Do **not** share confidential data with anyone outside the company.
• Do **not** copy or store confidential files on insecure devices (e.g., personal phones, external drives).
column4: Violations can lead to legal exposure, loss of reputation, and termination.

column3:
• **Password‑protect** the laptop and any associated accounts.
• Never leave the laptop **unattended** in public or unsecured locations.
• Install **security updates** (OS, browsers, applications) as soon as they are released.
• Connect to the corporate network **only through secure, private networks** (e.g., VPN).
• Follow all **encryption, anti‑malware, and password‑management** instructions that came with the device.
• Enable **disk encryption** and any other mandated data‑loss‑prevention (DLP) tools.
column4: Ensures that if the device is lost or stolen, the data remains unreadable and the system cannot be easily compromised.

column3:
• Treat remote work **exactly like office work** with respect to security, confidentiality, and equal‑opportunity policies.
• Follow the **Remote Working** guidelines (e.g., request approval, adhere to schedule limits).
column4: Guarantees consistent protection of data regardless of location.

column3:
• Company‑issued devices must have **Data‑Loss‑Prevention** controls in place.
• If you ever leave the company, **iCIMS data** (or other protected data) must be removed according to termination timelines.
• Personal devices **must not** be used to access customer data unless approved and monitored by Information Security.
• Personal devices **must not** connect directly to corporate or production networks; they should use a separate guest network when feasible.
column4: Reduces risk of data exfiltration from unmanaged devices.

column3:
• If the laptop is **stolen or damaged**, report it **within 24 hours** to the appropriate channel.
• File a police affidavit (if required) and forward a copy to the company.
column4: Enables rapid response, possible device tracking, and mitigation of data breach risk.

column3:
• Use **strong, unique passwords** and change them regularly.
• Be vigilant for **phishing or malware‑laden emails**; do not open suspicious attachments or links.
• Avoid playing games, excessive texting, or any non‑work activity that could expose the device to risk while on company time.
column4: Maintains overall security hygiene.

column1: ### Quick Checklist for Your Remote Session
1. **Start of day** – Verify laptop is password‑protected, encrypted, and VPN is active.
2. **During work** – Use only secure Wi‑Fi (or wired) connections; keep the screen locked when away.
3. **Handling data** – Store confidential files only on the encrypted drive; do not copy to USB sticks or personal cloud services.
4. **End of day** – Log out of all corporate accounts, lock the laptop, and store it in a safe location.
5. **If something goes wrong** – Report loss, damage, or a suspected security incident immediately (within 24 h).

By following the above responsibilities, you help protect the company’s sensitive employee, financial, and customer information while complying with the organization’s security and confidentiality policies.",7,5,6,12.594,1,0.6667,0.2857,1.0,0.7039
102,Can I use my company email to advertise my personal business?,medium,negative,Employee-Handbook.pdf,[233],Employee-Handbook,"[232, 234, 233, 230, 236, 251, 252]","## Short answer

**No – you may not use your company e‑mail to advertise your personal business** unless you have explicit authorization. Doing so is considered *unauthorized marketing content*, which is prohibited by the corporate e‑mail policy.
## Why the policy blocks this use

column3: Relevant rule(s)
column4: How it applies to advertising a personal business

column3: “You can use your email for personal reasons as long as you keep it safe, and avoid spamming and disclosing confidential information.”
column4: Advertising a personal business is a form of marketing. If the e‑mail is sent to coworkers, clients, or external contacts without permission, it is **spam** and **unauthorized marketing**.

column3: “Avoid… Sending unauthorized marketing content or emails.”
column4: Your personal‑business promotion would be **unauthorized marketing content** because the company e‑mail system is intended for work‑related communication, not personal commercial promotion.

column3: “Intentionally spamming other people’s emails, including your coworkers.”
column4: Mass‑mailing a promotion to colleagues or external parties would be considered spamming.

column3: “Signing up for illegal, unreliable, disreputable or suspect websites and services.”
column4: Using the corporate e‑mail to promote a personal venture could expose the company to reputational risk if the business is later deemed disreputable.

column1: ## What you *can* do instead
- **Use a personal e‑mail address** for any marketing or advertising of your own business.
- **Seek written permission** from your manager or the HR/Legal department if you believe a specific e‑mail is essential for a business‑related reason.
- **Keep personal e‑mail activity separate** from corporate systems to avoid accidental policy violations.
## Recommended next steps
1. **Stop any draft or scheduled e‑mail** that advertises your personal business using the corporate address.
2. **Switch to your personal e‑mail account** for all promotional communications.

3. If you think the promotion could benefit the company (e.g., a side‑project that aligns with company goals), **request formal approval** in writing before sending anything from the corporate mailbox.

**Bottom line:** The corporate e‑mail policy explicitly forbids sending unauthorized marketing content. Advertising your personal business via the company e‑mail would violate that rule, so you should not do it unless you obtain explicit authorization.",6,4,7,8.326,1,1.0,0.1429,0.3333,0.5

103,"If I witness workplace harassment involving my manager, who should I report it to?",medium,scenario,Employee-Handbook.pdf,[221],Employee-Handbook,"[222, 237, 221, 236, 220, 223, 239]","## Who to Report Workplace Harassment Involving Your Manager

column3: Recommended Reporting Channel

column2: **Harassment (verbal, psychological, sexual, or any other form) committed by a manager**
column3: **Human Resources (HR)** – your report will be kept confidential and investigated with discretion.

column2: **Severe physical violence (e.g., use of a lethal weapon) involving a manager**
column3: First call **building security** for immediate safety, then also inform **HR**.

column2: **If you are unsure whether the behavior qualifies as harassment**
column3: Start with **HR**; they can clarify the policy and guide you on next steps.

column1: ### Why HR Is the Correct Point of Contact
- The policy states:
> “Report to HR if you suspect or know that someone is being violent. Your report will be confidential and we will investigate the situation with discretion.”
- For harassment (including sexual harassment) the guidance is:

> “If you’re being harassed … you can choose to talk to any of these people: … **Your manager** … If customers, stakeholders or team members are involved in your claim, you may reach out to your manager.”

However, when the **manager is the alleged harasser**, you cannot use the manager as a reporting channel. The policy repeatedly instructs employees to **report harassment to HR** and to “report it to HR” for any inappropriate jokes, gossip, or other harassing behavior.
### Steps to Take When Reporting to HR
1. **Document the Incident** – note dates, times, locations, what was said or done, and any witnesses.
2. **Contact HR** – use the designated HR contact method (email, phone, internal portal) as provided by your company.
3. **Maintain Confidentiality** – the policy guarantees that your disclosure will remain confidential.
4. **Follow Up** – HR may request additional information or arrange a meeting; cooperate as needed.
### Additional Safety Measures (if needed)
- **If the situation escalates to physical danger** (e.g., threats with a weapon), **call building security immediately** for personal safety, then still file a report with HR.
- **If you feel unsafe confronting the manager directly**, avoid direct confrontation and go straight to HR.
**Bottom line:**

When you witness workplace harassment involving your manager, **report it directly to HR** (and, in cases of imminent physical danger, also alert building security). HR will handle the investigation confidentially and take appropriate action.",7,4,6,10.853,1,1.0,0.1429,0.3333,0.5
104,How do the Work From Home and Remote Working policies differ in terms of approval and eligibility?,hard,comparison,Employee-Handbook.pdf,"[249, 250]",Employee-Handbook
column3: IT-Security-Policy,"[249, 250, 128, 122, 211, 190, 218]","## Work‑From‑Home (WFH) vs. Remote‑Working Policies

column1: **Key differences in **approval process** and **eligibility criteria** are summarised below.**

column3: **Work‑From‑Home (WFH)**
column4: **Remote Working**

column3: Occasional tele‑commuting for employees whose role does **not require physical presence**.
column4: Working from a non‑office location **temporarily (up to 2 weeks)** or **permanently**.

column3:
• Normally **1 day per week**.
• More days can be arranged after manager discussion.
column4:
• **Maximum of 2 consecutive weeks per year** for office‑based staff (temporary).
• Permanent remote work is possible but subject to security & policy compliance.

column3:
• Job duties allow remote execution.
• No special personal circumstance required.
column4:
• **New parent** or **short‑term disability** are explicit eligibility reasons.
• Other reasons require manager approval.

column3:
• Notify your **manager** **via HRIS** **at least 2 days in advance**.
• You may set a **recurring WFH day**.
• In emergencies, you may start WFH immediately but must **call/email the manager** (or HR if the manager is in a different time‑zone).
column4:
• Submit a **remote‑working request through HRIS** **at least 1 week in advance**.
• Manager must approve the request.
• For permanent remote work, you must also agree to follow the company’s **security, confidentiality, and equal‑opportunity** policies.

column3:
• Primary approval/notification to the **direct manager**.
• HR is contacted only if the manager is unavailable (different time‑zone) or in emergencies.
column4:
• **Manager approval** is required for all remote‑working requests.
• HR processes the request and ensures compliance with broader policies.

column3: • If you need **more than the standard 1 day/week**, you must **talk to your manager** to arrange extra tele‑commuting days.
column4: • No provision for extending beyond the **2‑week limit** unless you transition to **permanent remote status**, which then follows the same policy requirements as any remote employee.

column3:
• Use a **fast, secure internet connection** and **secure devices**.
• Choose a quiet, distraction‑free workspace.
column4: • Must adhere to the same **security, confidentiality, and equal‑opportunity** standards as office‑based staff (especially for permanent remote work).

column1: ### Summary of Differences
- **Approval Timing**:
- *WFH*: 2‑day notice to manager (via HRIS).
- *Remote*: 1‑week notice to manager (via HRIS).
- **Eligibility Basis**:
- *WFH*: Determined by the nature of the job; generally open to any eligible employee.

- *Remote*: Limited to specific personal circumstances (new parent, short‑term disability) or other manager‑approved reasons, with a hard cap of **2 consecutive weeks per year** for temporary remote work.
- **Process for Emergencies**:
- *WFH*: Can start immediately; must inform manager (or HR if manager unavailable).
- *Remote*: No explicit emergency provision; standard request process applies.
- **Duration & Frequency**:
- *WFH*: Ongoing, typically **1 day/week** (can be recurring).
- *Remote*: **Temporary** (max 2 weeks) or **permanent** (subject to policy compliance).

If you need further clarification on how to submit a request or which policy applies to your situation, please contact your **manager** or **HR** as indicated in the respective sections.",9,10,9,14.629,1,1.0,0.2857,1.0,1.0
105,What company policies should I keep in mind before posting company information on my personal social media account?,hard,multi_section,Employee-Handbook.pdf,"[219, 234]",Employee-Handbook
column2: IT-Security-Policy,"[234, 235, 218, 232, 219, 190, 204]","## Policies to Review Before Posting Company Information on Your Personal Social Media

column3: Key Requirements
column4: What to Do Before Posting

column3:
• Protect client, employee, partner, and company data.
• Do not disclose unpublished financials, customer lists, forecasts, or any “confidential” label items.
• Follow NDAs, non‑compete, and any signed confidentiality agreements.
column4:
• Verify that the information is **publicly released** or **officially approved**.
• If unsure, **ask your manager or the PR/Marketing department** before sharing.

column3: • Do not share trademarks, copyrighted material, or any proprietary content without permission.
column4: • Confirm that the content is **not protected IP** or that you have **explicit clearance** to use it.

column3: • Avoid defamatory, offensive, or derogatory statements about colleagues, clients, partners, or the company.
column4: • Ensure your post contains **no personal attacks** or false statements.

column3: • Personal accounts must be clearly distinguished from the company’s official voice.
column4: • Add a disclaimer such as **“Opinions are my own”** or **“These views do not represent [Company]”**.

column2: **Company Representation Guidelines** (when you *are* speaking on behalf of the company)
column3:
• Be respectful, polite, and patient.
• Stay within your field of expertise.
• Coordinate major‑impact content with PR/Marketing.
• Correct or remove misleading information quickly.
column4: • Even on a personal account, treat any company‑related post as a **representation**; follow the same standards.

column3:
• Do not use personal devices to record or transmit confidential information.
• Do not upload or download illegal, obscene, or disreputable material.
column4: • Ensure the post does **not contain screenshots, documents, or media** that could expose confidential data.

column2: **Employee Handbook / Corporate Email Policy** (relevant for sharing links or documents)
column3:
• Avoid spamming, illegal sites, or unauthorized marketing content.
• Do not disclose confidential information via email links.
column4: • If you share a link, verify it is **company‑approved** and does not lead to restricted content.

column1: ### Step‑by‑Step Checklist
1. **Identify the Content**
- Is the information **publicly announced** (press release, official website, etc.)?
- Does it contain **confidential labels** (e.g., “unpublished financial information,” “customer list”)?
2. **Check IP & Copyright**
- Does the post include **trademarks, logos, proprietary images, or excerpts** from internal documents?
3. **Confirm Authorization**
- Have you **asked your manager or PR/Marketing** for clearance if the information is not already public?
4. **Add a Disclaimer**
- Include a clear statement that the view is **personal** and **not the company’s official position**.
5. **Review for Harassment/Defamation**
- Ensure the wording is **neutral, factual, and respectful**.
6. **Secure the Posting Device**
- Use a **company‑approved device or a secure personal device**; avoid screenshots of confidential screens.
7. **Post and Monitor**
- After posting, be ready to **correct or remove** any misinformation promptly.
### Quick Reference
- **Do NOT** share:
- Unreleased product details, financial forecasts, customer lists, internal strategies.
- Trademarked logos or copyrighted material without permission.
- Any content that could be seen as defamatory or harassing.
- Verify public status or obtain clearance.
- Use a disclaimer.
- Follow confidentiality, IP, and anti‑harassment policies.

> **Bottom line:** Before posting any company‑related information on your personal social media, treat it as if you were speaking on behalf of the organization. Verify that the content is public or approved, protect confidential and proprietary data, add a personal‑account disclaimer, and ensure the post complies with the company’s confidentiality, IP, anti‑harassment, and social‑media representation policies.",8,8,8,9.897,1,1.0,0.2857,1.0,0.8503

106,A patient is about to receive a medication they've never taken before. What should the healthcare team do before giving it and what follow-up is expected afterwards?,hard,multi_section,Medication-Administration-Policy.pdf,"[276, 281, 287, 288]",policy-and-procedures-of-medication-administration-and-follow-up,"[276, 280, 288, 286, 281, 274, 278]","## 1. Pre‑administration actions  *(what the team must do before giving a medication that is new to the patient)*

column3: What to do
column4: Policy reference

column3:
• Check the patient’s ID bracelet.
• Ask the patient to state name & birth‑date.
• Match the medication order with the ID and with the patient’s reported allergies.

• Perform a **triple‑check** of the label.
• Retrieve and prepare the exact medication ordered.
• Verify label against the physician’s order; never use medication prepared by another person.

• Check concentration on the label.
• Compare the prepared dose with the order.
• Triple‑check all calculations and have a second nurse verify them.
• Confirm the dose is within the appropriate range for the patient.
• Verify the correct route (IV, PO, etc.) and the scheduled time.
• Do **not** document administration until the medication has actually been given.

• Inform the patient (or responsible party) of the medication name, purpose, and possible side‑effects.
• Ask about known drug allergies.

• Perform a brief assessment to confirm the medication is safe and appropriate for this patient (e.g., labs, vitals, contraindications).
• If unsafe, notify the ordering physician/clinical pharmacist and document the decision.
• Ensure the practitioner understands the medication’s monitoring requirements (e.g., labs, vital signs) and is satisfied that these will be carried out.
• If the patient or legal representative refuses, explain consequences, verify understanding, notify the physician, and document the refusal.
• The admin/Pharmacy in‑charge should have allocated resources and communicated the role of each staff member for this new‑medication episode.

column1: **Key point from policy:**
> *“The hospital Nursing and Pharmacy department must have a process for monitoring the response to the first dose of medications that are new to the patient.”* (Section 5.2)
## 2. Immediate post‑administration follow‑up  *(what is expected right after the first dose)*

column3: Details
column4: Policy reference

column3:
• Observe the patient for any immediate side‑effects or adverse reactions.
• Record any findings.
• Assess whether the intended therapeutic effect is beginning to appear (e.g., pain relief, vital‑sign change).

• Document the patient’s response, including any adverse events, effectiveness, and comparison to baseline status.
• Ensure documentation occurs **after** the medication is given.
• If any suspicion of an adverse event or unexpected response, inform the treating physician and/or clinical pharmacist promptly.
• For serious side‑effects, consider withholding the medication and follow the Yellow‑card/ADR reporting process.
• Spend additional bedside time after the first dose (as per 7.2.4) and follow any specific monitoring requirements (labs, vitals, etc.) outlined in the medication’s protocol.

column1: ## 3. Ongoing follow‑up (beyond the immediate period)
1. **Regular Re‑assessment** – Continue to monitor the patient according to clinical need (Section 5.3).
2. **Adjust Therapy** – If the drug is ineffective or risks outweigh benefits, stop or modify therapy following the appropriate protocol (Section 5.3).
3. **Physician Communication** – Physicians must keep patients informed about the need for follow‑up care and any required changes to the treatment plan (Section 5.4).
4. **Documentation Updates** – All subsequent observations, interventions, and decisions must be entered into the patient’s record (Section 6.1.10).
### Quick Checklist for a “new‑to‑patient” medication
```text
[ ] Verify patient identity & allergies
[ ] Triple‑check medication label & dose
[ ] Confirm route, time, and calculations
[ ] Provide patient education (purpose, side‑effects)
[ ] Perform safety assessment (labs, vitals)
[ ] Ensure monitoring plan is in place
[ ] Administer medication
[ ] Observe for adverse effects & effectiveness
[ ] Document response & any actions taken
[ ] Notify physician/pharmacist if concerns arise
[ ] Continue scheduled monitoring & follow‑up
**Bottom line:**

Before giving a medication that the patient has never taken, the team must complete the full “right‑*” checks (patient, medication, dose, route, time, documentation, education, assessment, evaluation, and monitoring plan). After administration, they must promptly assess for side‑effects and therapeutic effect, document the findings, and communicate any issues to the physician or clinical pharmacist, with ongoing monitoring until the medication’s safety and efficacy are confirmed.",7,4,8,13.763,1,0.75,0.4286,1.0,0.7366

107,"I noticed a patient's allergy just before giving the medicine, and the prescription is also difficult to read. What should I do before administering anything?",hard,scenario,Medication-Administration-Policy.pdf,"[280, 286, 287, 288]",policy-and-procedures-of-medication-administration-and-follow-up,"[278, 287, 280, 277, 284, 286, 279]","## Immediate Action – **Do NOT administer the medication**
Both the newly‑identified allergy and the illegible prescription are **critical safety concerns**.
According to the policy (sections 6.1.1‑6.1.6, 6.4.6, 6.4.9), you must stop the administration process until the issues are resolved.
## 1. Verify the Patient’s Allergy (Right Allergy / Right Education)

column3: What to do
column4: Policy reference

column3: **Check the patient’s allergy list on the chart** and compare it with the medication you are about to give.
column4: 6.1.1.4 – Verify patient’s allergies with chart and with patient.

column3: **Ask the patient (or responsible party) to state any known drug allergies** and confirm the information verbally.
column4: 6.1.1.2 – Ask patient to state name and birth date (applies to allergy confirmation as well).

column3: If the medication **contains an allergen** or the patient reports an allergy, **do not proceed**.
column4: 6.1.8.1 – Properly assess the patient to determine if medication is safe.

column3: **Document** the allergy finding and the decision to withhold the medication.
column4: 6.1.8.3 – Document that medication was not administered and the reason.

column3: **Notify the prescribing physician (or clinical pharmacist)** of the allergy and request an alternative order.
column4: 7.1.1 – Physician shall monitor and evaluate; staff nurse shall contact prescriber for unclear orders (6.4.6).

column1: ## 2. Resolve the Illegible Prescription (Right Medication / Right Order)

column3: What to do
column4: Policy reference

column3: **Confirm that the prescription is legible and valid**. If any part is unreadable, treat it as illegible.
column4: 6.4.6 – Check if the prescription is legible and valid.

column3: **Do NOT prepare or administer** the medication until clarification is obtained.
column4: 6.1.2.6 – Never administer medication prepared by another person; also implied by “check label with physician’s orders”.

column3: **Contact the prescriber** (physician, authorized nurse, or pharmacist) **immediately** to verify the order.
column4: 6.4.6 – Contact prescriber for clarification; 6.2.1 – Staff nurse shall ensure they can clearly read and understand the orders.

column3: If the prescriber is unavailable, **escalate to the Clinical Pharmacy department** for verification.
column4: 7.1.1 – Physician monitors; staff nurse contacts pharmacy professionals for incomplete/unclear orders.

column3: Once the order is clarified, **perform a triple‑check of the medication label** against the clarified order.
column4: 6.1.2.1‑6.1.2.5 – Triple check label, compare with order.

column3: **Document** the clarification process (who was contacted, time, and the clarified order).
column4: 6.4.9 – Documentation required at time of administration; also 6.1.8.3 for documentation of any deviation.

column1: ## 3. Additional Safeguards Before Administration
1. **Second‑nurse verification** – After the allergy and order issues are resolved, have another qualified nurse **re‑check the calculations, dose, route, and time** (6.1.3.4, 6.1.3.5).
2. **Right Time / Right Route** – Verify date, time, and route as per sections 6.1.5 and 6.1.4.
3. **Patient education** – Inform the patient about the medication, its purpose, and possible side effects (6.1.6).
## 4. Summary Checklist

**No.** According to the medication‑administration policy a student nurse may **only** give medication **while a registered nurse is present and directly supervising** the activity.
### Relevant Policy Extracts

column3: Requirement
column4: What it means for a student nurse

column3: “A practitioner in training/Student Nurse can only administer medicines **under the direction and direct supervision of a registered nurse**. The Staff Nurse remains responsible for ensuring that the correct procedure takes place.”
column4: The student must have the RN **in the room and actively supervising** the whole administration.

column3: “Medicines must only be prepared, checked or administered … by a competent health‑care staff only from the categories of Doctors / Nursing / Pharmacy professionals.”
column4: A student nurse is not a fully‑qualified nursing professional; they require supervision.

column3: “Both these persons must remain present **throughout the entire procedure**.”
column4: For controlled drugs the RN (and a witness) must stay in the room for the whole process.

column1: ### Interpretation
- **Direct supervision** = the registered nurse must stay in the room, watch the preparation, checking, and administration, and be able to intervene immediately if needed.
- **Briefly leaving the room** breaks the “throughout the entire procedure” requirement and the “direct supervision” requirement.
### Conclusion

A student nurse administering medication while the registered nurse steps out of the room **does not comply** with the policy. The RN must remain present until the medication has been fully administered and documented. After the dose is actually given, you must complete the **post‑administration documentation and evaluation** as required by the “Right Evaluation” and “Right Documentation” sections.
## What the Policy Requires

column3: Requirement
column4: Why it matters

column3: *Never document before medication is administered.*
column4: Guarantees the record reflects what truly happened and prevents falsified or premature entries.

column3:
1. Assess patient for any adverse side effects.
2. Assess effectiveness of the medication.
3. Compare the patient’s prior status with post‑medication status.
4. Document the patient’s response.
column4: Ensures safe, effective care and provides a traceable audit trail.

column3: Inform the patient about the medication, side effects, and allergies before giving it.

column1: ## Correct Workflow for a Busy Shift
1. **Prepare & Verify (Right 1‑5)**
- Confirm patient identity, medication, dose, route, time, and allergies.
- Perform required double‑checks (e.g., triple‑check calculations, witness for controlled drugs).
2. **Educate & Obtain Consent**
- Tell the patient what is being given, possible side effects, and confirm no known allergies.
3. **Administer the Medication**
- Give the dose **first**, then move immediately to documentation.
4. **Post‑Administration Evaluation (Right 9)**
- **Assess** for any immediate adverse reactions.
- **Evaluate** therapeutic effect (e.g., pain relief, vital‑sign changes).
- **Compare** the patient’s status before and after the dose.
5. **Document (Right 10)** – *after* the dose:
- Record the exact time of administration.
- Note the **patient’s response** (e.g., “no adverse effects; pain reduced from 8/10 to 4/10”).
- Sign/initial the entry (or use electronic signature) in the patient’s record.
- If a dose was **skipped or refused**, document the reason per 6.1.8.3 and notify the prescriber.
6. **Report Any Adverse Event** (per 7.2.5)
- If an unexpected reaction occurs, notify the treating physician/clinical pharmacist promptly and record the event.
## Practical Tips for Busy Shifts

column3: Recommended Practice
Use a **real‑time electronic medication administration record (eMAR)** that locks the “document” button until the “administer” action is confirmed.
Pair with a colleague for the **witness** step (especially for controlled drugs) and to double‑check calculations.
Pause the workflow, re‑verify the “Five Rights,” then proceed; avoid pre‑documenting as a memory aid.
Review the **Audit Tool (Appendix 2)** regularly; items 5 and 1 specifically check that documentation occurs **immediately after** administration.

column1: ## Bottom Line
- **Pre‑documenting** a medication **is prohibited** by the policy.
- **After** you give the medication, you must **evaluate the patient** (adverse effects, effectiveness, status change) and **document** those findings **immediately** in the patient’s record.

1. **Prescriber (Doctor)** writes a legible, counter‑signed CD prescription.
2. **Pharmacy/Nurse** prepares the CD, inspects it (6.2), and locks any surplus in the CD cabinet (6.4.7).
3. **Authorized staff nurse** (administering) and a **second registered nurse** (witness) **verify**:
- Prescription validity (6.4.6)
- Patient identity (6.4.8)
4. **Administration** is performed by the staff nurse while the witness remains present (6.4.5).

- Initial/sign the prescription chart (6.4.9)
